assessment.rationale: Pressure-sensing implants exist in small studies but no one has shown they stop glaucoma, so the Main KPI of 76,000,000 patients protected is open work. The EYEMATE-SC suprachoroidal telemetric sensor has been implanted in 24 patients with three-year follow-up: no dislocation, position drift from 1.6 to 2.1 millimetres over 1,080 days, no astigmatic effect, good agreement with Goldmann tonometry, high adherence, 15 moderate adverse events with one possibly sensor-related, and the authors state the effect on progression and quality of life needs further study; a 2026 review lists Eyemate-IO, Eyemate-SC, IOP Connect and Q Smart with cost, regulatory approval and long-term validation as open barriers (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=%28%22eyemate%22%20OR%20%22intraocular%20pressure%20sensor%22%29%20AND%20implant%20AND%20glaucoma&format=json&pageSize=5&resultType=core). The registry confirms the scale: ARGOS-IO in 16 and ARGOS-SC in 24 patients, the rest contact-lens sensors. The harder half is that pressure control alone does not stop the disease: a 2026 study found 19 percent of eyes progressing fast despite office pressure at target, and reviews state neurodegeneration often persists after pressure lowering. Open code is eight small monitoring apps and non-contact prototypes (https://api.github.com/search/repositories?q=glaucoma+intraocular+pressure+monitoring&per_page=10&sort=stars). Honest limit: implanted telemetric pressure sensing is already demonstrated prior art, so a sensor-only task is a known answer; the open work is turning continuous pressure data into prevented blindness.

additionalSearches.query: implanted intraocular pressure sensors in glaucoma
additionalSearches.finding: EYEMATE-SC studies: 24 patients implanted with three-year follow-up, 13 analysed for positional stability (drift 1.6 to 2.1 millimetres by day 1080, no dislocations), no significant astigmatism or acuity change versus 24 canaloplasty controls, 15 moderate adverse events after the early phase with one possibly sensor-related, good agreement with Goldmann tonometry and high adherence. The authors say the effect on progression and quality of life needs further study. A 2026 review cites cost, regulatory approval, long-term validation and workflow as barriers; no record states a CE mark.

The implanted sensor studies are ARGOS-IO long-term safety and performance in 16 patients with primary open-angle glaucoma and ARGOS-SC suprachoroidal performance and safety in 24 patients, both completed and both device studies without a phase. The remaining entries are contact-lens sensors and unrelated monitoring studies. Nothing approaches population scale.

additionalSearches.query: glaucoma progression despite controlled intraocular pressure
additionalSearches.finding: A 2026 Am J Ophthalmol study of 67 eyes in 36 people found 13 fast progressors (19 percent of eyes) of whom only 3 were above target at office visits, and 22 of 59 eyes at target had water-drinking peaks above 21 mm Hg with faster loss. Reviews state that although lowering pressure remains the primary intervention, neurodegeneration often persists, and nicotinamide evidence is insufficient for neuroprotection. Sensing pressure is not the same as preventing blindness.

Eight repositories, top-starred at 11: a medication and pressure tracking app, and several student non-contact or IoT pressure-estimation prototypes (ESP32, Arduino, image-based). No open implanted sensor or closed-loop treatment system.
